Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Jack Markell]] was term-limited and could not run for re-election to a third term in office. Democratic congressman [[John Carney (Delaware politician)|John Carney]] defeated Republican state senator [[Colin Bonini]] in a landslide. The primaries were held on May 3, 2016. Republican lieutenant governor Eric Holcomb won the race with 51.4% of the vote. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] Governor [[Mike Pence]] was running for reelection to a second term in office until July 15, 2016, when then-Republican presidential nominee [[Donald Trump]] selected Pence as his vice presidential running mate.{{cite news|title=Donald Trump selects Mike Pence as VP|url=http://www.cnn.com/2016/07/14/politics/donald-trump-vice-presidential-choice/|access-date=July 15, 2016}} As Pence was barred by Indiana law from simultaneously running for both offices, he subsequently withdrew from the gubernatorial election.{{cite web |url=http://www.wdrb.com/story/32454202/mike-pence-officially-withdraws-from-indiana-governors-race |title=Mike Pence officially withdraws from Indiana governor's race |publisher=WDRB.com |date=July 15, 2016 |access-date=July 15, 2016 |archive-date=November 10, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181110075857/http://www.wdrb.com/story/32454202/mike-pence-officially-withdraws-from-indiana-governors-race |url-status=dead }} Pence went on to be elected [[Vice President of the United States]]. He was replaced on the ballot for governor by his former [[running mate]], incumbent lieutenant governor [[Eric Holcomb]], who was selected by the [[Indiana Republican Party|Indiana Republican State Committee]] as the nominee on July 26, 2016.{{cite news|url=http://www.indystar.com/story/news/politics/2016/07/26/live-updates-indiana-republicans-meet-today-pick-pences-replacement/87540124/|title=Indiana GOP panel nominates Eric Holcomb for governor|newspaper=[[The Indianapolis Star]]|last1=Eason|first1=Brian|last2=Tony|first2=Cook|last3=Briggs|first3=James|date=July 26, 2016|access-date=July 26, 2016}} Holcomb later selected [[Indiana State Auditor|State Auditor]] [[Suzanne Crouch]] on August 1, 2016, to be his running mate as the nomination for lieutenant governor was made vacant by the decision of Holcomb to seek the gubernatorial nomination; she was confirmed at a subsequent meeting of the Indiana Republican State Committee later that day. [[John R. Gregg|John Gregg]], the former [[Speaker of the Indiana House of Representatives]], was the Democratic nominee. Gregg previously ran for governor in [[2012 Indiana gubernatorial election|2012]] but was defeated by Pence. Under Indiana law, Pence was unable to run for both governor and vice president simultaneously; he therefore withdrew from the gubernatorial election, creating a vacancy on the Republican ticket. On July 26, the chairman of the [[Indiana Republican Party]], [[Jeff Cardwell]], announced that [[Eric Holcomb]] had been nominated by the Indiana Republican State Committee to replace Pence on the ballot for governor. The vote totals were not released. Holcomb later selected [[Suzanne Crouch]] on August 1, 2016, to be his running mate as the nomination for lieutenant governor was made vacant by the decision of Holcomb to seek the gubernatorial nomination; she was then confirmed by the Committee at a meeting later that day.{{cite web|url=http://fox59.com/2016/08/01/holcomb-to-introduce-crouch-as-his-running-mate-in-governors-race/|title=Holcomb introduces Crouch as his running mate in governor's race|publisher=[[WXIN|Fox 59]]|date=August 1, 2016|access-date=August 2, 2016|archive-date=August 2, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160802185857/http://fox59.com/2016/08/01/holcomb-to-introduce-crouch-as-his-running-mate-in-governors-race/|url-status=dead}} ===Candidates=== ====Replacement nominee==== * [[Eric Holcomb]], [[Lieutenant Governor of Indiana]] ** Running mate: [[Suzanne Crouch]], [[Indiana State Auditor]] ====Eliminated at state committee selection==== * [[Susan Brooks]], U.S. Representative and former [[United States Attorney]] for the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of Indiana|Southern District of Indiana]]{{cite web|url=http://www.ibj.com/articles/59509-holcomb-brooks-are-in-bosma-is-out-of-race-to-be-gop-gubernatorial-nominee|title=Holcomb, Rokita, Brooks in; '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of Missouri|Governor]] | before_election = [[Jay Nixon]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Eric Greitens]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsMO}} The '''2016 Missouri gubernatorial election''' was held on November 8, 2016, to elect the [[governor of Missouri]], concurrently with the [[2016 United States presidential election|2016 U.S. presidential election]], as well as [[United States Senate elections, 2016|elections]] to the [[2016 United States Senate election in Missouri|United States Senate]], [[United States House of Representatives elections, 2016|elections]] to the [[2016 United States House of Representatives elections in Missouri|United States House of Representatives]], and various [[United States elections, 2016#State elections|state]] and [[United States elections, 2016#Local elections|local elections]]. The primaries were held on August 2. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Jay Nixon]] was term-limited and could not run for re-election to a third term in office.{{cite news|author=Bill McClellan|title=Bill McClellan: Jay Nixon could make presidential bid in 2016|url=http://www.stltoday.com/news/local/columns/bill-mcclellan/bill-mcclellan-jay-nixon-could-make-presidential-bid-in/article_21c02e01-1968-5a2e-8758-f6d0f2405cb3.html|access-date=March 3, 2013|newspaper=St. Louis Post-Dispatch|date=October 5, 2012}} State [[List of Attorneys General of Missouri|Attorney General]] [[Chris Koster]] and businessman, author and former [[United States Navy SEALs|U.S. Navy SEAL]] [[Eric Greitens]] won the Democratic and Republican primaries, respectively.{{cite web|last=Held|first=Kevin S.|url=http://fox2now.com/2016/08/02/koster-wins-democratic-gubernatorial-primary/|title=Koster wins Democratic gubernatorial primary|work=[[KTVI]]|date=August 2, 2016|access-date=August 2, 2016}}{{cite web|last1=Lieb|first1=David A.|last2=Ballentine|first2=Summer|title=Ex-Navy SEAL Eric Greitens wins Missouri governor primary|url=http://www.wrcbtv.com/story/32602092/ex-navy-seal-eric-greitens-wins-missouri-governor-primary|work=[[WRCB]]|date=August 2, 2016|access-date=August 2, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160804213247/http://www.wrcbtv.com/story/32602092/ex-navy-seal-eric-greitens-wins-missouri-governor-primary|archive-date=August 4, 2016|url-status=dead|df=mdy-all}} On election day, November 8, 2016, the [[Associated Press]] declared Greitens the winner of the election, and Koster conceded shortly after.{{cite web|url=http://fox2now.com/2016/11/08/eric-greitens-declares-victory-in-missouri-gubernatorial-race/|title=Eric Greitens declares victory in Missouri gubernatorial race|date=9 November 2016}} This was the first gubernatorial election in Missouri since [[1968 Missouri gubernatorial election|1968]] in which the winner was from a different party from the presidential candidate who won the popular vote in the concurrent election{{Efn|While [[Hillary Clinton]] lost the election to [[Donald Trump]], she won the popular vote.|name=|group=}}, and the first since [[1940 Missouri gubernatorial {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Steve Bullock (American politician)|Steve Bullock]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Steve Bullock (American politician)|Steve Bullock]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) | turnout = 74.44%{{increase}}2.26{{cite web |url=https://sosmt.gov/elections/voter-turnout/|title=Montana Voter Turnout|newspaper=Montana Secretary of State - Christi Jacobsen|date=February 22, 2018 |access-date=2022-05-26}} }} {{ElectionsMT}} The '''2016 Montana gubernatorial election''' took place on November 8, 2016, to elect the [[Governor of Montana|governor]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of Montana|lieutenant governor of Montana]], concurrently with the [[2016 United States presidential election in Montana|presidential election]], as well as [[United States Senate elections, 2016|elections]] to the [[United States Senate]] and [[United States House of Representatives elections, 2016|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]] and various [[United States elections, 2016#State elections|state]] and [[United States elections, 2016#Local elections|local elections]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Steve Bullock (American politician)|Steve Bullock]] won re-election to a second term in office with 50.3% of the vote by a 3.9% margin, defeating [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[Greg Gianforte]], who later won Montana's governorship in [[2020 Montana gubernatorial election|2020]] when Bullock was term-limited. In the concurrent presidential election, [[Hillary Clinton]] lost Montana by more than 20%, with Bullock thus over-performing her vote share by more than 14% and her margin of defeat by more than 24%. As of 2026, this is the most recent election where a Democrat won the Governor's office and/or a state level office. ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== * [[Steve Bullock (American '''Tie''': {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Pat McCrory]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Roy Cooper]] | after_party = [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] }} {{ElectionsNC}} The '''2016 North Carolina gubernatorial election''' was held on November 8, 2016, concurrently with the [[2016 United States presidential election|2016 U.S. presidential election]], as well as [[2016 United States Senate elections|elections]] to the [[United States Senate]] and [[2016 United States House of Representatives elections|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]] and various [[2016 United States elections#State elections|state]] and [[2016 United States elections#Local elections|local elections]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] state Attorney General [[Roy Cooper]] won his first term in office, narrowly defeating [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] incumbent [[Pat McCrory]]. Primary elections were held March 15.{{Cite web |url=http://www.wral.com/north-carolina-primaries-now-on-march-15-with-bill-signing/14938667/ |title=WRAL: North Carolina primaries officially on March 15 with signing |access-date=October 1, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151002070437/http://www.wral.com/north-carolina-primaries-now-on-march-15-with-bill-signing/14938667/ |archive-date=October 2, 2015 |url-status=dead }} Both McCrory and Cooper won their primaries by overwhelming margins.{{cite news|url=http://www.newsobserver.com/2014/12/02/4370719_gov-pat-mccrory-launches-2016.html|title=Gov. Pat McCrory launches 2016 campaign|newspaper=The News & Observer|date=December 2, 2014|access-date=December 5, 2014|archive-date=December 26, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141226023618/http://www.newsobserver.com/2014/12/02/4370719_gov-pat-mccrory-launches-2016.html|url-status=dead}} [[Lon Cecil]], a consultant and electrical engineer, was the [[Libertarian Party (United States)|Libertarian]] nominee. This race was expected to be among the most competitive in the country in the [[2016 United States gubernatorial elections|2016 gubernatorial election cycle]].{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2015/12/competitive-governor-races-2016-217111|title=Top 10 governors races of 2016| website=[[Politico]] |date=December 29, 2015 |access-date=November 22, 2016}} On election night, the race was too close to call, with Cooper leading by fewer than 5,000 votes out of more than 4.6 million cast.{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/11/09/us/politics/governors-races-statehouses-eric-holcomb.html|title=In North Carolina, a Governor's Race Is Too Close to Call|date=November 9, 2016|work=The New York Times|access-date=November 22, 2016}} That lead eventually widened to 10,281 votes. Cooper claimed victory that night, with thousands of provisional ballots still yet to be counted, saying, "We have won this race." However, McCrory refused to concede, claiming that the race was still too close to call and the winner had not yet been determined. He cast doubt on the authenticity of 90,000 late-arriving votes from Durham County, which put Cooper in the lead. McCrory's campaign filed complaints alleging [[voter fraud]] in over 50 counties. Both campaigns anticipated a protracted legal battle over the results.{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/the-fix/wp/2016/11/10/this-2016-race-still-isnt-over-and-its-about-to-get-ugly/|title=The North Carolina governor's race still isn't over. And it's about to get even uglier.| newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |access-date=November 22, 2016}} On November 22, 2016, McCrory formally requested a statewide recount;[http://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2016/nov/23/nc-gov-pat-mccrory-wont-concede-seeks-recount/ N.C. governor seeks recount amid voter-fraud complaints, won't concede] once all ballots are counted, North Carolina election law allows either candidate to request a recount if the margin is fewer than 10,000 votes. On November 30, 2016, the North Carolina State Board of Elections ordered a recount of certain votes in Durham County.{{Cite web |url=http://abc11.com/politics/state-board-orders-recount-of-94000-durham-county-votes/1631935/ |title=State Board Orders Recount of 94,000 Durham County Votes |access-date=December 1, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161201201500/http://abc11.com/politics/state-board-orders-recount-of-94000-durham-county-votes/1631935/ |archive-date=December 1, 2016 |url-status=dead }} The recount was slated to be completed on December 5, 2016. However, when early results made it apparent that the margin would not change, McCrory conceded the race to Cooper on the afternoon of December 5. This was the first time since North Carolina governors became eligible for immediate reelection in 1976 that a sitting officeholder was defeated in a bid for a second term and the only North Carolina gubernatorial election since [[1896 North Carolina gubernatorial election|1896]] in which neither major party nominee received over 50% of the vote.{{cite news|url=http://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/election/article118942758.html|title=Gov. On election night, as votes were tallied, Cooper held an early lead, but was overtaken by McCrory around 9:30 pm, and McCrory held the lead for most of the evening. Shortly before midnight, McCrory held a 60,000 vote lead until a block of 90,000 votes from [[Durham County, North Carolina|Durham County]] was added to the total, putting Cooper back in the lead by fewer than 5,000 votes out of 4,500,000 cast.{{cite web|url=http://abc11.com/politics/cooper-claiming-victory-in-governors-race/1596556/|title=Cooper claiming victory in Governor's race|first=Jonah|last=Kaplan|website=ABC11 News|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210927184540/https://abc11.com/politics/cooper-claiming-victory-in-governors-race/1596556/|archive-date=September 27, 2021|date=November 8, 2016|access-date=November 22, 2016|url-status=dead}} Both candidates addressed supporters around 12:30 am; Cooper declared victory, while McCrory vowed the race was not over and that every vote needed to be counted. Under North Carolina state law, absentee ballots postmarked on or before election day must be counted, and military and overseas ballots accepted through November 17 must also be counted.Nigel Duara, [http://www.latimes.com/nation/la-na-north-carolina-governor-20161118-story.html North Carolina governor's race still undecided with thousands of votes to be finalized], ''Los Angeles Times'' (November 18, 2016). Additionally, election administrators "must decide the eligibility of more than 60,000 provisional ballots and the validity of thousands of challenged votes." This process, plus a protracted legal challenge from the McCrory campaign, was likely to leave the election result not formally decided for some time after election day. McCrory's campaign said that it had "grave concerns over potential irregularities in Durham County." [[Republican Party of North Carolina]] Chairman Robin Hayes called Cooper's declaration of victory "rude and grossly premature." On November 10, 2016, both campaigns announced they had retained attorneys in anticipation of a protracted legal battle: Cooper hired lawyers from [[Washington state|Washington-based]] firm [[Perkins Coie]] (including [[Marc Elias]]Virginia Bridges, Colin Campbell & Craig Jarvis, [http://www.newsobserver.com/news/local/community/durham-news/article115681693.html Appeal planned after Durham County dismisses demand for hand recount], ''News & Observer'' (November 17, 2016).), while McCrory hired lawyers from [[Virginia]]-based firm Holtzman Vogel Josefiak. Once all ballots are counted, North Carolina election law allows either candidate to request a recount if the margin is fewer than 10,000 votes. On November 12, the [[general counsel]] of the Durham County Republican Party filed a formal protest with the Durham County Board of Elections alleging "malfeasance" in the tallying of votes in Durham County and calling for a recount.{{cite web|url=http://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/state-politics/article114262543.html|title=Provisional ballot count offers few hints in governor race|access-date=November 22, 2016}} McCrory's campaign said that the 90,000 votes added to the total late on election night appeared to have come from corrupted memory cards. A campaign spokesman said, "What transpired in Durham County is extremely troubling and no citizen can have confidence in the results at this point in time." On November 14, [[WRAL-TV|WRAL]] reported that there was speculation among political operatives about whether the race could possibly be contested and handed to the [[North Carolina General Assembly]] to determine the winner, as was done in 2005, when the General Assembly made [[June Atkinson]] the winner of a disputed election for the office of [[North Carolina Superintendent of Public Instruction]].{{cite web|url=http://www.wral.com/could-nc-lawmakers-choose-the-next-governor-/16234656/|title=Could NC lawmakers choose the next governor? :: WRAL.com|last=WRAL|date=November 14, 2016|access-date=November 22, 2016}} North Carolina House [[Speaker of the North Carolina House of Representatives|Speaker]] [[Tim Moore (North Carolina politician)|Tim Moore]] said getting the General Assembly involved would be "an absolute last resort".{{cite web|url=http://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/state-politics/article114980628.html|title=Could NC legislators decide governor race? 'Last resort,' House speaker says|access-date=November 22, 2016}} Also on November 14, WRAL reported that the State Bureau of Investigation was investigating whether crimes were committed in the mishandling of 1,000 ballots in the March 2016 primaries in Durham County, the likely epicenter of the battle over the gubernatorial race.{{cite web|url=http://www.wral.com/durham-defends-handling-of-90k-ballots-in-nc-governor-s-race/16234762/|title=SBI investigating mishandled primary ballots in Durham :: WRAL.com|last=WRAL|date=November 14, 2016|access-date=November 22, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161119123641/http://www.wral.com/durham-defends-handling-of-90k-ballots-in-nc-governor-s-race/16234762/|archive-date=November 19, 2016|url-status=dead}} The Durham County electoral board chairman said there was no connection between the investigation and the gubernatorial race. On November 15 [[Bladen County, North Carolina|Bladen County]] Soil and Water Conservation District Supervisor [[McCrae Dowless]], a Republican and the incumbent for reelection, filed a protest with that county's board of elections over several hundred absentee ballots cast for Cooper and other Democrats, claiming that they were fraudulent; on the basis of similarity of the handwriting with which they were filled out. In his initial filing, Dowless claimed corroboration by a handwriting expert. The complainant had initially expressed concerns about voter fraud related to his own reelection campaign, and before election day.{{cite web|url=http://www.wect.com/story/33718588/hundreds-of-fraudulent-cooper-ballots-discovered-challenged-in-bladen-county|title=Protests filed in Bladen and 11 other counties over alleged fraudulent absentee ballots|author=WECT Staff|access-date=November 22, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161116164226/http://www.wect.com/story/33718588/hundreds-of-fraudulent-cooper-ballots-discovered-challenged-in-bladen-county|archive-date=November 16, 2016|url-status=dead}}{{cite web|url=http://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/state-politics/article115013278.html|title=Bladen County votes scrutinized|access-date=November 22, 2016}}{{cite web|url=http://www.journalnow.com/news/state_region_ap/the-latest-state-board-investigates-bladen-absentee-ballots/article_59361bd9-d574-5ef7-a425-18a9fec2fefc.html|title=The Latest: State board investigates Bladen absentee ballots|access-date=November 22, 2016|archive-date=November 17, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161117163307/http://www.journalnow.com/news/state_region_ap/the-latest-state-board-investigates-bladen-absentee-ballots/article_59361bd9-d574-5ef7-a425-18a9fec2fefc.html|url-status=dead}} The McCrory campaign alleged that the ballots were filled out by paid employees of the Bladen County Improvement Association PAC, a [[political action committee]] that received funding from the [[North Carolina Democratic Party]]. The complaint alleged that one person served as a witness for at least 67 mail-in absentee ballots, and the same person appeared to have filled out the selections on 71 ballots.{{cite web|url=https://gallery.mailchimp.com/67f0361f3af450acafd9830a7/files/ElectionProtestForm_Bladen_Co_Soil_Water_Signed.pdf|title=Bladen Protest|access-date=November 22, 2016}} It said there were at least 250 questionable ballots connected to five people paid by the Bladen County Improvement Association PAC. That organization has responded that the people involved were volunteers with their get-out-the-vote effort, and that the only payments made to them were small stipends for expenses incurred as part of that activity; such as food and gas costs. The McCrory campaign stated, "A massive voting fraud scheme has been uncovered in Bladen County."{{cite web|url=https://www.foxnews.com/politics/voter-fraud-complaints-emerge-in-tight-nc-gov-race|title=Voter fraud complaints emerge in tight NC gov race|first=Joseph|last=Weber| website=[[Fox News]] |date=November 16, 2016|access-date=November 22, 2016}} In response, the Cooper campaign stated: "Governor McCrory has set a new standard for desperation in his attempts to undermine the results of an election he lost."[http://myfox8.com/2016/11/17/gov-mccrory-protests-votes-in-50-counties/ Gov. McCrory protests votes in 50 counties], WGHP (November 17, 2016). On November 16, the McCrory campaign announced it had filed election protests alleging fraud in 11 more counties.{{cite web|url=http://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/state-politics/article115143258.html|title=McCrory team: Election protests filed in 12 counties|access-date=November 22, 2016}}{{cite web|url=http://www.wfmynews2.com/news/local/mccrory-campaign-filing-protests-in-12-counties/353374505|title=McCrory Campaign Now Protesting Votes In 50 Counties|last=TEGNA|access-date=November 22, 2016|archive-date=November 18, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161118040347/http://www.wfmynews2.com/news/local/mccrory-campaign-filing-protests-in-12-counties/353374505|url-status=dead}} On November 17, the McCrory campaign announced the number of counties in which it had filed protests alleging voter fraud had grown to 50 counties,Jim Bradley, [http://www.wsoctv.com/news/local/undecided-gubernatorial-race-presents-problems-for-candidates/468201866 Gov. Pat McCrory protesting vote counts in 50 counties] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161118101345/http://www.wsoctv.com/news/local/undecided-gubernatorial-race-presents-problems-for-candidates/468201866 |date=November 18, 2016 }}, WSOC (November 18, 2016). which the [[Associated Press]] reported were "without offering detailed proof." Every county election board in the state has three members: two Republican appointees and one Democrat.Bill Chappell, [https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2016/11/19/502719928/n-c-challenger-to-gov-mccrory-remains-in-lead-as-final-ballots-counted N.C. Challenger to Gov. McCrory Remains In Lead As Final Ballots Counted], NPR (November 19, 2016). Durham County has been seen as the most pivotal county, as it has the most votes at stake. On November 16, the Durham County Board of Elections voted 2–1 to hold an evidentiary hearing on election protest about the ballots in Durham County.[http://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/state-politics/article115137173.html#wgt=trending Durham County board to hold hearing on election protest], ''News & Observer'' (November 16, 2016). At the hearing on November 18, the board unanimously dismissed the protest, with the board's Republican chairman, William Brian Jr., saying that all the evidence shows that the count is correct.{{cite news |last=Robinson |first=Gary D. |title=Democrat Attorney General Roy Cooper increases his ballot lead over Gov. Pat McCrory in the North Carolina governor's race |date=November 18, 2016 |work=The Charlotte Observer |url=https://www.charlotteobserver.com/news/local/article115794358.html}} By November 18, Cooper's unofficial advantage over McCrory had grown to about 6,600 votes, out of almost 4.7 million cast. On November 20, the state Board of Elections held an emergency meeting. They declined a McCrory campaign petition for the state board to take jurisdiction over all 50 county election protests, except for the one in Bladen County, which they took over.{{cite web|url=http://www.wral.com/election-board-weighing-mccrory-request-in-governor-s-race/16258266/|title=N Carolina election board takes Bladen protest, not others :: WRAL.com|last=WRAL|date=November 20, 2016|access-date=November 22, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161122025826/http://www.wral.com/election-board-weighing-mccrory-request-in-governor-s-race/16258266/|archive-date=November 22, 2016|url-status=dead}} They decided to convene another meeting on November 22 to issue guidance to county boards on how to handle the protests.{{cite web|url=http://myfox8.com/2016/11/20/nc-board-of-elections-to-hold-emergency-meeting-on-sunday/|title=NC Board of Elections votes to reconvene Tuesday|date=November 20, 2016|access-date=November 22, 2016}} On November 22, the McCrory campaign formally requested a statewide recount. Also on November 22, the [[Civitas Institute]] filed a federal lawsuit seeking an [[injunction]] to delay the State Board of Elections' count of ballots of unverified same-day registrants, alleging that there is not enough time to verify the eligibility of voters who registered to vote on election day.[http://www.greensboro.com/news/local_news/civitas-institute-lawsuit-wants-same-day-vote-count-delayed/article_1fda4bfd-34aa-5525-a63c-9587fdda16dc.html Civitas Institute lawsuit wants same-day vote count delayed] Civitas said that neither the McCrory campaign nor the state Republican Party were involved in the lawsuit.{{cite news |title=Civitas sues to stop final NC vote count, cites concerns about same-day registration |work=The Charlotte Observer |date=November 22, 2016 |url=https://www.charlotteobserver.com/news/politics-government/election/article116403158.html}} Civitas cited a 2012 review conducted by the state Board of Elections that found 2.44% of voters who used same-day registration in 2012 failed the verification process, but the process was not completely finished when the ballots were counted. A court hearing is scheduled for December 8.[https://www.nytimes.com/2016/11/29/us/north-carolina-governor-race.html?_r=0 In North Carolina, No End in Sight to Governor’s Race] On November 26, the Durham County Republican Party's general counsel asked the state Board of Elections to hold an expedited hearing on his appeal of the Durham County Board of Elections' refusal to conduct a recount of that county's votes.{{cite news |title=NC elections board could consider key ballot appeal this week |work=The Charlotte Observer |date=November 27, 2016 |url=https://www.charlotteobserver.com/news/politics-government/article117403393.html}} The campaign stated they would withdraw their request for a statewide recount if a manual recount of Durham County votes produced the same results as were reported on election day.[http://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/state-politics/article117284658.html McCrory will withdraw recount demand if Durham votes recounted] On November 30, the State Board of Elections ordered a recount of the Durham County votes. The recount was to be completed by 7 p.m. on December 5. However, by that morning, early results showed no change in the tally. McCrory announced on his campaign's YouTube channel that he was conceding the race to Cooper, saying that it was now clear that "the majority of our citizens had spoken." ===Official results=== 2016 North Dakota gubernatorial election.title: 2016 North Dakota gubernatorial election
2016 North Dakota gubernatorial election.text:
{{Short description|none}} {{for|related races|2016 United States gubernatorial elections}} {{Use American English|date=January 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=September 2023}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2016 North Dakota gubernatorial election | country = North Dakota | type = presidential | ongoing = no | previous_election = 2012 North Dakota gubernatorial election | previous_year = 2012 | next_election = 2020 North Dakota gubernatorial election | next_year = 2020 | election_date = November 8, 2016 | image1 = File:DougBurgum 2018 (cropped-1).jpg | image_size = 150x150px | nominee1 = '''[[Doug Burgum]]''' | party1 = Republican Party (United States) | popular_vote1 = '''259,863''' | percentage1 = '''76.52%''' | running_mate1 = '''[[Brent Sanford]]''' | image2 = 3x4.svg | nominee2 = [[Marvin Nelson]] | party2 = North Dakota Democratic–Nonpartisan League Party | popular_vote2 = 65,855 | percentage2 = 19.39% | running_mate2 = [[Joan Heckaman]] | map_image = {{switcher |[[File:2016 North Dakota gubernatorial election results map by county.svg|250px]] |County results |[[File:ND Governor 2016.svg|250px]] |Precinct results}} | map_caption = '''Burgum:''' {{legend0|#E27F7F|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#D72F30|70–80%}} {{legend0|#C21B18|80–90%}} {{legend0|#A80000|>90%}}
'''Nelson:''' {{legend0|#A5B0FF|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} {{legend0|#3933e5|80–90%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Jack Dalrymple]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Doug Burgum]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsND}} The '''2016 North Dakota gubernatorial election''' was held on November 8, 2016, to elect the [[Governor of North Dakota|governor]] and [[lieutenant governor of North Dakota]], concurrently with the [[2016 United States presidential election|2016 U.S. presidential election]], [[2016 United States Senate elections|elections]] to the [[United States Senate]], [[2016 United States House of Representatives elections|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]], and various [[2016 North Dakota elections|state and local elections]]. This would have been the first time North Dakotans selected a governor under new voter ID requirements, in which a student ID was insufficient identification to vote,{{cite news|last1=Watts|first1=Adam|last2=Lyden|first2=Grace|title=ID law may complicate voting for North Dakota students|url=http://www.inforum.com/news/3980757-id-law-may-complicate-voting-north-dakota-students|access-date=March 9, 2016|work=[[Forum of Fargo-Moorhead]]|date=March 9, 2016}} but a court ruling in August 2016 struck down the provision; the election was held under the 2013 rules.{{cite news|last1=Childress|first1=Sarah|title=North Dakota's Voter ID Law Is Latest to Be Overturned|url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/frontline/article/north-dakotas-voter-id-law-is-latest-to-be-overturned/|access-date=September 22, 2016|work=[[Frontline (U.S. TV series)|Frontline]]|publisher=[[WGBH-TV]]|date=August 2, 2016}} The primaries took place on June 14. This is the first open seat election since [[2000 North Dakota gubernatorial election|2000]]. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[Jack Dalrymple]] announced that he would not run for re-election to a second full term in office.{{cite web|url=http://kfgo.com/news/articles/2015/aug/24/dalrymple-wont-run-for-re-election/|title=Dalrymple won't run for re-election|publisher=[[KFGO (AM)|KFGO]]|date=August 24, 2015|access-date=August 24, 2015|archive-date=August 25, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150825161426/http://kfgo.com/news/articles/2015/aug/24/dalrymple-wont-run-for-re-election/|url-status=dead}} Businessman [[Doug Burgum]] (R) defeated state Representative [[Marvin Nelson]] (DNPL) in the general election to become the new governor of North Dakota. ==Background== In December 2010, Republican Governor [[John Hoeven]] resigned after being [[2010 United States Senate election in North Dakota|elected]] to the U.S. Senate. Jack Dalrymple, the lieutenant governor, was sworn in as governor and was elected to a full term [[North Dakota gubernatorial election, 2012|in 2012]]. In August 2015, Dalrymple announced that he would not run for re-election to a second full term in office. ==Republican primary== The North Dakota Republican Party endorsed [[North Dakota Attorney General]] [[Wayne Stenehjem]] at their April 2–3 state convention. However, ballot access was actually determined by the June 14 primary election, which former Microsoft executive [[Doug Burgum]] won in an [[Upset (competition)|upset]].{{cite web|url=http://www.grandforksherald.com/news/politics/3924505-doug-burgum-announces-bid-north-dakota-governor|title=Doug Burgum announces bid for North Dakota governor|work=[[Grand Forks After the first round, all candidates would remain on the ballot, but after subsequent rounds of voting, the recipient of the lowest number of votes would be removed. The first candidate to receive more than half the cast vote would receive the state party endorsement. After no candidate received the majority in the first round, a second round of voting was completed, in which enough delegates voted for Attorney General Wayne Stenehjem to give him the endorsement The primaries were held on September 13. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Maggie Hassan]] was eligible to run for re-election to a third term in office, but she instead [[2016 United States Senate election in New Hampshire|successfully ran for the U.S. Senate]] against incumbent [[Kelly Ayotte]].{{cite news|url=http://www.rollcall.com/news/for_nh_republicans_pain_is_probably_temporary-228773-1.html |title= For N.H. With a margin of 2.27%, this election was the second-closest race of the [[2016 United States gubernatorial elections|2016 gubernatorial election cycle]], behind only [[2016 North Carolina gubernatorial election|the election in North Carolina]]. ==Background== Governor [[Maggie Hassan]], the incumbent from the Democratic Party, declined to run for reelection, choosing to seek a U.S. Senate seat instead. Both major parties had multiple declared candidates, leading to [[Partisan primary|primary election]]s that were held September 13, 2016. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = [[Governor of Oregon|Governor]] | before_election = [[Kate Brown]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Kate Brown]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsOR}} The '''2016 Oregon gubernatorial special election''' took place on November 8, 2016, to elect the [[Governor of Oregon]], concurrently with the [[2016 United States presidential election in Oregon|2016 U.S. presidential election]], as well as elections for the [[United States Senate elections, 2016|U.S. Senate]] and [[United States House of Representatives elections, 2016|U.S. House of Representatives]], [[2016 United States gubernatorial elections|other gubernatorial elections]] and various [[United States elections, 2016#State elections|state]] and [[United States elections, 2016#Local elections|local elections]]. The election determined who would fill the remaining two years of the term of Democratic governor [[John Kitzhaber]], who was re-elected in 2014 and resigned in February 2015. Incumbent Democratic governor [[Kate Brown]], who as [[Oregon Secretary of State]] succeeded to the governorship, ran for election to the office. In primary elections held on May 17, Brown easily captured the Democratic nomination, and the Republicans picked [[Salem, Oregon|Salem]] [[oncologist]] [[Bud Pierce]]. Brown won the election and became the first openly [[LGBT]] person elected to a term as governor in U.S. history. This election was the first time since [[1990 Oregon gubernatorial election|1990]] that a woman was elected Governor of Oregon. [[Incumbent]] [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Gary Herbert]] ran for re-election to a second full term in office.{{cite news|url=http://www.sltrib.com/sltrib/politics/58113805-90/herbert-governor-2016-gov.html.csp |title=Governor Herbert says he will run for re-election in 2016 |work=The Salt Lake Tribune |date=June 25, 2014 |access-date=August 22, 2014}} Republican challenger [[Jonathan E. Johnson]] defeated Herbert in the state convention to secure a spot on the primary ballot,{{cite web | url=http://fox13now.com/2016/04/23/gov-gary-herbert-forced-into-primary-election-with-jonathan-johnson/ | title=Fox 13 Utah: Governor Gary Herbert Forced Into Primary Election by Jonathan "JJ" Johnson| date=23 April 2016}} but Herbert won the June 28, 2016 primary and secured the nomination.{{cite news |last=Roche |first=Lisa |date=June 28, 2016 |title=Gov. Gary Herbert wins GOP nomination |url=http://www.deseretnews.com/article/865657103/Gov-Gary-Herbert-holds-big-lead-over-Jonathan-Johnson-in-early-results.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160630190134/http://www.deseretnews.com/article/865657103/Gov-Gary-Herbert-holds-big-lead-over-Jonathan-Johnson-in-early-results.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=June 30, 2016 |newspaper=Deseret News |access-date=June 29, 2016 }} The Democratic party nominated former [[CHG Healthcare Services]] CEO Mike Weinholtz at the Utah Democratic convention in April. Herbert won the general election, defeating Weinholtz by a large margin.{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/elections/2016/results/utah-governor-herbert-weinholtz|title=Utah Governor Results: Gary Herbert Wins|work=The New York Times |date=August 1, 2017|via=NYTimes.com}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.thespectrum.com/story/news/2016/11/09/herbert-wins-re-election-governor/93531242/|title=Herbert wins re-election as governor|first=Michelle L.|last=Price|website=The Spectrum}} ==Background== Republican Governor [[Jon Huntsman, Jr.]] resigned in August 2009 to become [[United States Ambassador to China]] and Lieutenant Governor Herbert succeeded him. He was elected to serve out the remainder of Huntsman's term in a [[Utah gubernatorial special election, 2010|2010 special election]] and was re-elected to a full four-year term [[Utah gubernatorial election, 2012|in 2012]]. ==Republican nomination== Former Speaker of the [[Utah House of Representatives]] [[Rebecca D. Lockhart]] was widely believed to be a potential Republican candidate, but she died of a rare neurodegenerative brain disease in January 2015.{{cite news|url=http://fox13now.com/2015/01/17/becky-lockhart-utahs-first-female-house-speaker-dies/|title=Becky Lockhart, Utah's first female House speaker, dies|work=FOX13|date=January 17, 2015|access-date=January 18, 2015}} Incumbent governor Gary Herbert won the June 28, 2016 primary, defeating Overstock.com Chairman Jonathan Johnson. ===Candidates=== ====Declared==== * [[Gary Herbert]], incumbent governor * [[Jonathan E. 2016 Vermont gubernatorial election.text:

'''Minter:''' {{legend0|#A5B0FF|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996E2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674DE|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584CDE|70–80%}}
'''''Tie:''''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Peter Shumlin]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Phil Scott]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsVT}} The '''2016 Vermont gubernatorial election''' took place on November 8, 2016, and elected the [[governor of Vermont]], concurrently with the [[2016 United States presidential election|2016 U.S. presidential election]], [[2016 United States Senate elections|elections]] to the [[United States Senate]] in other states, [[2016 United States House of Representatives elections|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]], and various [[2016 United States elections#State elections|state]] and [[2016 United States elections#Local elections|local elections]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Peter Shumlin]] was eligible to run for re-election to a fourth term in office, but opted to retire instead.{{cite web|url=http://www.sevendaysvt.com/OffMessage/archives/2015/06/08/shumlin-announces-he-wont-seek-reelection-in-2016|title=Shumlin Announces He Won't Seek Reelection in 2016|work=[[Seven Days (newspaper)|Seven Days]]|author1=Paul Heintz|author2=Terri Hallenbeck|date=June 8, 2015|access-date=June 13, 2015}} The primaries were held on August 9.{{cite web | title=Elections – Vermont Secretary of State | website=sec.state.vt.us | date=2016-04-25 | url=https://www.sec.state.vt.us/elections/candidates.aspx | access-date=2016-05-27 | archive-date=2016-06-01 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160601103059/https://www.sec.state.vt.us/elections/candidates.aspx | url-status=dead }} Former [[Vermont Agency of Transportation]] Secretary [[Sue Minter]] won the Democratic nomination, and Lieutenant Governor [[Phil Scott]] won the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] primary,{{cite web | last1=Freese | first1=Alicia | last2=Hallenbeck | first2=Terri | title=Live Coverage of the Vermont Primary Results | website=Seven Days | date=8 August 2016 | url=http://www.sevendaysvt.com/OffMessage/archives/2016/08/08/tune-in-tuesday-for-seven-days-primary-coverage | access-date=10 August 2016}} with Scott defeating Minter in the general election. This was the first gubernatorial election in Vermont in which the winner was of a different party than the incumbent president since 1992. ==Background== Two-term Democratic governor [[Peter Shumlin]] ran for re-election in [[2014 Vermont gubernatorial election|2014]] and was widely expected to win easily. However, he only took a plurality of the vote, 46.36%, to Republican [[Scott Milne]]'s 45.1%, and thus the result was decided by the [[Vermont General Assembly]]. The Assembly picked Shumlin by 110 votes to 69. Shumlin announced in June 2015 that he would not run for a fourth term.{{cite news|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/2015/06/08/shumlin-decided-against-2016-re-election/28690591/ |title=Shumlin decides against 2016 re-election bid |work=Burlington Free Press |date=June 8, 2015 |access-date=June 8, 2015}} Vermont and [[New Hampshire]] are the only states in the country whose governors are elected every two years. ==Democratic primary== In August, Vermont House Speaker [[Shap Smith]] announced that he would be a candidate,{{cite news |date=August 14, 2015 |title=Shap Smith wants to Succeed Peter Shumlin as next Vermont Governor |url=http://www.timesargus.com/article/20150814/NEWS03/708149951 |newspaper=The Times Argus |location=Barre, VT |access-date=July 2, 2016 |archive-date=February 15, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160215202213/http://www.timesargus.com/article/20150814/NEWS03/708149951 |url-status=dead }} but ended his candidacy in November 2015, after his wife was diagnosed with breast cancer.{{cite news |last=Burbank |first=April |date=November 17, 2015 |title=Shap Smith Suspends Campaign for Governor |url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/2015/11/17/shap-smith-to-make-campaign-announcement/75932852/ |newspaper=Burlington Free Press |location=Burlington, VT}} In September, [[Matt Dunne]] announced that he would also be a candidate.{{cite news |last=Gram |first=David |agency=Associated Press |date=September 2, 2015 |title=Google Executive Matt Dunne Running for Vermont Governor |url=http://www.pressherald.com/2015/09/02/google-executive-matt-dunne-running-for-vermont-governor/ |newspaper=Portland Press Herald |location=Portland, ME}} Also in September, former state legislator [[Sue Minter]], then serving as Vermont's [[Vermont Agency of Transportation|Secretary of Transportation]], announced that she would resign her position in order to join the Democratic race.{{cite news |last=Hallenbeck |first= Terri |date=September 10, 2015 |title=Sue Minter to Run for Vermont Governor |url=http://www.sevendaysvt.com/OffMessage/archives/2015/09/10/sue-minter-to-run-for-vermont-governor |newspaper=Seven Days |location=Shelburne, VT}} Former ambassador [[Peter Galbraith]] announced '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = [[Governor of Washington|Governor]] | before_election = [[Jay Inslee]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Jay Inslee]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{Elections in Washington State}} The '''2016 Washington gubernatorial election''' was held on November 8, 2016. Under Washington's [[top-two primary]] law, all candidates appear on the same ballot, regardless of party. In the August 2 primary, residents voted for one of several candidates from a range of party affiliations. The top two finishers, incumbent Governor [[Jay Inslee]] (Democratic){{cite news|url=http://blog.seattlepi.com/seattlepolitics/2014/10/21/stockpiling-for-2016-gov-inslee-stages-quiet-2014-fundraiser/ |title=Stockpiling for 2016? Gov. Inslee stages quiet 2014 fundraiser|access-date=October 21, 2014|publisher=Seattle Pi|date=October 26, 2014}} and Port of Seattle Commissioner [[Bill Bryant (politician)|Bill Bryant]] (Republican), moved on to the November general election, which Inslee won. [[Pacific County, Washington|Pacific County]] voted for a Republican gubernatorial candidate for the first time since [[1964 Washington gubernatorial election|1964]] and [[Grays Harbor County, Washington|Grays Harbor County]] did so for the first time since [[1924 Washington gubernatorial election|1924]]. As of {{CURRENTYEAR}}, this was the last gubernatorial election in Washington in which the margin of victory was within single digits. ==Background== Democratic governor [[Christine Gregoire]] declined to seek a third term in 2012. Democratic former U.S. Representative [[Jay Inslee]] was elected to succeed her, defeating Republican [[Rob McKenna]], the outgoing [[List of Attorneys General of Washington|Attorney General of '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Earl Ray Tomblin]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Jim Justice]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsWV}} The '''2016 West Virginia gubernatorial election''' took place on November 8, 2016, to elect the [[List of Governors of West Virginia|governor of West Virginia]], concurrently with the [[2016 United States presidential election in West Virginia|2016 U.S. presidential election]], as well as [[2016 United States Senate elections|elections]] to the [[United States Senate]] in other states and [[2016 United States House of Representatives elections|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]], and various [[2016 United States elections#State elections|state]] and [[2016 United States elections#Local elections|local elections]]. The primaries were held on May 10. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Earl Ray Tomblin]] was barred from running for a second full term. He had ascended to the governorship upon [[Joe Manchin]]'s resignation in 2010, won a [[2011 West Virginia gubernatorial special election|2011 special election]] to complete the term, and won a full term in [[2012 West Virginia gubernatorial election|2012]]. Under the [[Constitution of West Virginia|West Virginia Constitution]], a partial term counts toward the limit of two consecutive terms. Democratic nominee [[Jim Justice]], a [[hotelier]] and [[coal baron]], won the open seat with a plurality of the vote, defeating Republican state senator [[Bill Cole (West Virginia politician)|Bill Cole]] and former state senator [[Charlotte Pritt]], who ran as a member of the Mountain Party. As of 2024, this is the last time a Democrat was elected governor of West Virginia, the last West Virginia gubernatorial race where the winner won less than 61% of votes, and the last West Virginia gubernatorial race where the winner did not win every county. Justice switched parties in August 2017 and was re-elected as a Republican in [[2020 West Virginia gubernatorial election|2020]], giving Republicans the governorship for the first time since 2001 and a trifecta in the state for the first time since 1931.{{Cite web |last=Staff |first=WSAZ News |date=2020-11-04 |title=Justice wins second term as W.Va. governor |url=https://www.wsaz.com/2020/11/04/justice-wins-second-term-as-wva-governor/ |access-date=2023-07-08 |website=www.wsaz.com |language=en}} ==Background== In November 2010, Democratic governor [[Joe Manchin]] resigned after being [[United States Senate special election in West Virginia, 2010|elected]] to the U.S. Senate. Earl Ray Tomblin, the [[President of the West Virginia Senate|president]] of the [[West Virginia Senate]] (with the honorary title of lieutenant governor), became acting governor, won an [[2011 West Virginia gubernatorial special election|October 2011 special election]] to complete the term, and won a full term in the [[West Virginia gubernatorial election, 2012|regularly scheduled 2012 election]]. Tomblin was ineligible to run for re-election in 2016, as the [[Constitution of West Virginia]] limits governors to two consecutive terms regardless of whether they are full or partial terms. However, governors are re-eligible after four years out of office.{{cite news|last=Miller|first=Tom|title=2016 race for governor could be crowded|url=http://lincolnjournalinc.com/race-for-governor-could-be-crowded-p6727-87.htm|access-date=March 4, 2013|newspaper=The Lincoln Journal|archive-date=February 22, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140222044609/http://lincolnjournalinc.com/race-for-governor-could-be-crowded-p6727-87.htm|url-status=dead}}{{cite news|last=King|first=Joselyn|title=Tomblin, Maloney win nominations|url=http://wetzelchronicle.com/page/content.detail/id/504690/Tomblin--Maloney-Win-Nominations.html|access-date=March 3, 2013|newspaper=Wetzel Chronicle|date=May 18, 2011}} After publicly speculating he would run for his former office, Manchin was considered a heavy favorite in the 2016 race, but he announced on April 19, 2015, that he would remain in the Senate instead.{{cite news|last=Ramsey|first=Pam|title=Manchin says he'll stay in Senate, forgoes governor bid|url=https://www.journal-news.net/page/content.detail/id/632744.html|access-date=April 19, 2015|newspaper=[[The Journal (West Virginia newspaper)|The Journal]]|date=April 19, 2015|archive-date=April 27, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150427111616/https://www.journal-news.net/page/content.detail/id/632744.html|url-status=dead}} ==Democratic primary== {{Infobox election | election_name = 2016 West Virginia gubernatorial election Democratic primary | country = West Virginia | type = primary | ongoing = no | election_date = May 10, 2016 | image1 = [[File:Governor Jim Justice 2017.jpg|x125px]] | candidate1 = '''[[Jim Justice]]''' | color1 = 3333FF | image2 = [[File:R Booth Goodwin US Attorney.jpg|x125px]] | candidate2 = [[Booth Goodwin]] | color2 = 3333FF | map_image = West Virginia Democratic gubernatorial primary results by county, 2016.svg | map_size = 250px | map_caption = Results by county.
